Even compression across every frequency in the track.

The sound is taken apart into individual tones, and each one's loudness is evened out by its own envelope. Loud sounds don't drag the rest down, and the compressor treats every sound equally steadily, whatever the loudness of any frequency in the mix. With a loud kick, low end or midrange, it squeezes the lows and the highs just the same.

The threshold is automatic: it sets itself from the loudest sound and moves along with the track. The release is automatic too (AUTO): the plugin measures how fast the sounds fade out and sets the time itself. Every tone — kick, drums or vocal — is compressed the same way, then the level is raised back automatically, which gives you a well and densely compressed track.
Works beyond mastering too, on any track or bus, with a higher CPU load.
One number for the whole sound.
An ordinary compressor is output = gain × signal. Every classic complaint follows from that:
The detector is blind — the whole spectrum is collapsed into one number, so a kick and a vocal of the same amplitude are indistinguishable to it.
The kick drags everything with it — the gain drops, and the hats, the vocal and the reverb tails dive with it. That is pumping.
Attack fights punch — one envelope has to serve both the transient and the body.
The bass gets dirty — the gain moves, and sidebands grow around a 50 Hz kick. The compressor ruins the very thing it was evening out.

Since the first compressors of the 1930s the principle has stayed the same: one gain for the whole signal. HOUZY drops it. Every tone gets its own envelope, so pumping, the attack-versus-punch trade-off and sidebands on the bass don't arise in the first place.

ACR — a clipper that stops chopping the highs.

An ordinary clipper slices the top off the waveform. A slice is abrupt and its error is broadband, so every kick hit subtracts that error from the hats, the vocal and the reverb tails. Hence the classic problem with clipped house: the harder you drive the kick, the duller and grittier the top end gets. Oversampling makes the error clean, but does not change where it sits in the spectrum.

Instead of slicing, ACR subtracts a short pulse placed exactly at the peak. Its spectrum puts the distortion at the top, where the hats and the kick's attack mask it. The technique comes from LTE transmitters; the pulse kernel is designed from a psychoacoustic model of hearing.
ACR is the default. HI-Q — a conventional oversampled clipper — is the other position of the switch.
T8 — the half-wave limiter.
An ordinary limiter moves its gain whenever it needs to, often right in the middle of a wave. On a kick or a bass that bends the wave itself, and you hear it as grit inside every hit.
T8 changes its gain only where the wave crosses zero. Each half-wave of the kick and bass is lowered as one whole piece, so its shape stays exactly as it was. Only its height changes.
Our own design, new in HOUZY 5. In our kick tests about 5–6 dB cleaner than T6 at the same loudness. On the SMART | T6 | T8 switch.
Attack in wave cycles, release in beat fractions.

5 ms on a 50 Hz bass note is a quarter of its wave — the gain moves inside a single oscillation, exactly where a compressor dirties the low end. The same 5 ms on an 8 kHz hat is forty cycles. So attack is set in cycles: one knob gives 45 ms at 50 Hz and 1 ms at 8 kHz, never faster than half a cycle.

Release can be set two ways, click its label to switch. MS is plain milliseconds (default). NOTE is a fraction of a bar: release follows your project tempo, so a tempo change needs no re-tweaking. And AUTO listens to how fast the sounds in your track fade and sets the release to match.

How to Master Electronic Music with HOUZY | Manual
How to master electronic music with HOUZY
The HOUZY manual: where to start (AMOUNT at 15–30), what each control does to the sound, and how to fine-tune a track of electronic and dance music.
AMOUNT · INPUT · CYCLES · RELEASE
Two minutes from opening HOUZY to a dense, even track. The same guide is built into HOUZY, in the ACRONA card.
Mode
Pick HOUZY — it gives the best sound quality.
1. AMOUNT
Start with the AMOUNT knob. For a well-mixed track, 15 to 30 usually gives soft, moderate compression. For anything else, set it by ear.
2. INPUT
Once the compression feels right, raise INPUT while watching the LUFS meter. For a soft sound, −10 to −9 LUFS is enough.
3. CYCLES
For a soft kick, set it between 3 and 4.
4. RELEASE
Leave AUTO on: the plugin measures how fast the sounds in your track decay and sets the release for you.
5. BEAT or SMART
Choose by ear.
BEAT holds the release exactly as set: a steadier sound that pulses with the beat.
SMART treats the release as a maximum: a sound that fades out sooner is let go sooner. Airier and more natural.
Fine-tuning
DASH — if the compression sounds good but the track still isn't even enough, add some DASH.
UPWARD — lifts the quiet parts: reverb tails, air, the top end.
CLIP SHAPE — light saturation across the whole track. Loudness is matched automatically, so you hear the colour, not a volume boost.

ALL MIX — if the track sounds dense overall but, say, the highs or the mids stick out, switch on ALL MIX and pull that band down with its knob. To see which frequencies a band covers, rest the pointer on its knob for a couple of seconds — a tip shows the range.
Clipper: HI-Q or ACR
We recommend ACR, our own clipper. It moves the distortion to where the hit masks it, so the attacks stay clean. Still, it's a matter of taste — try both.
OVERSAMPLE
16x is plenty while you work; use 32x for the final render.
TRUE PEAK
The TP button sits on the OUTPUT knob. Turn it on when you export for streaming: it removes the inter-sample peaks that crackle after conversion to MP3/AAC.
In short
AMOUNT 15 to 30, CYCLES 3 to 4.
Raise INPUT if needed.
A little DASH and UPWARD to taste.
In ALL MIX, pull down whatever sticks out.
Done.

What is HOUZY?

HOUZY is a mastering compressor plugin (VST3 and AU) by ACRONA AUDIO. Instead of one gain for the whole mix, it gives every tone of the spectrum its own envelope, so a loud kick or bass does not pull the rest of the mix down: no pumping, a punchy kick, a clean low end. It was born in electronic and dance music and works on any genre.
A multiband helps, but only part of the way

Splitting the mix into 3–6 bands gives each band its own gain, so the kick no longer pulls down the hats. But inside a band nothing changes: the kick and the bass still share one gain, the low band still pumps, and the crossover filters shift the phase at every split.

Frequently asked questions
Does HOUZY pump?
No. There is no shared gain, so nothing can pump: every tone is compressed by its own envelope.
How is HOUZY different from a multiband compressor?
A multiband gives each band its own gain, but inside a band the kick and the bass still share it. HOUZY gives every tone its own gain, with no crossovers in the signal path.
Can I use HOUZY on single tracks, not only the master?
Yes, on any track or bus. HOUZY analyses every tone separately, so its CPU load is higher than an ordinary compressor's. Its latency is reported to the DAW and compensated automatically.
Which formats and DAWs does HOUZY support?
VST3 on Windows, VST3 and AU on macOS: Ableton Live, FL Studio, Cubase, Reaper, Bitwig, Logic Pro and other hosts that load VST3 or AU.

The best mastering compressor depends on the job: gluing a mix, controlling dynamics, or adding density without losing the transients. For electronic and dance music the main problem is pumping, which is why per-tone compressors such as HOUZY exist.
What to look for in a mastering compressor
Transparency — low distortion and no pumping on the kick and the bass.
Control — attack, release, ratio, a side-chain filter and mid/side options.
Level matching — auto gain, so you judge the sound and not the loudness.
Peak safety — a limiter or a true-peak stage for streaming and MP3 exports.
Cost to your workflow — latency, CPU load, price and licence terms.
